narrative:
Your law school application was denied because the model estimated a 91.7% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, that very high risk was treated as decisive, so you were not admitted.

The strongest influence was your third-year class standing: you were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. That placed you far below the typical admitted profile and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year class standing was the second most important factor, and it pointed the same way: you were also in the lowest decile, compared with an accepted-student average near the sixth decile. Together, these signals suggested sustained academic difficulty relative to successful applicants.

Your family income bracket was the third most influential factor. You reported an upper-middle income background, a common category among accepted students, but in your case this factor added a smaller push toward the failure prediction. Your LSAT score of 31, below the accepted average of about 37, and undergraduate GPA of 2.70, below the accepted average of about 3.23, reinforce the same concern.

Next, seek specific feedback from the admissions office, consider retaking the LSAT, and work with an advisor on a plan to demonstrate stronger academic readiness before reapplying.
